summary: Defines the MIME content type Message/CPIM, a message format for protocols that conform to the Common Profile for Instant Messaging. It wraps a message with headers describing sender, recipient and other details so it can pass between systems.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3862 defines the shape of an instant message when it has to be signed and encrypted from end to end. The message has two halves. The first is a set of headers describing who it is from, who it is to and when it was sent. The second is the content, wrapped as an ordinary MIME object.

The rules are strict on purpose. Headers cannot be reordered or rewritten on the way, control characters are escaped in a fixed way, and everything is in UTF-8, so that two ends compute the same signature over the same bytes.

questions: how are control characters escaped in cpim headers
why must cpim messages be immutable
subtitle: A canonical message format for instant messaging that can be signed and encrypted end to end.

tldr.problem: Instant messaging systems use many different protocols, and a message often has to pass through a gateway that speaks another one. RFC 2779 requires end-to-end signatures and encryption, and plain email-style message formats cannot provide them, because gateways rewrite headers and re-encode the content as they go.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3862 defines a MIME content type, Message/CPIM, with a fixed two-part shape: a set of message headers for the metadata, then an encapsulated MIME object for the content. The syntax is stricter than email's, headers are immutable in transit, and control characters are escaped so the exact bytes can be signed.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from August 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It registers the media type for limited use and defines seven headers, including one for extending the header namespace and one for insisting that the recipient understands a feature.

today: RFC 3862 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the Message/CPIM media type and of the urn:ietf:params:cpim-headers: namespace. The media type is registered for limited use.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The document defines the MIME content type Message/CPIM, a message format for protocols that conform to the Common Profile for Instant Messaging specification. It is a common message format for CPIM-compliant messaging protocols. While being prepared for CPIM, the format is quite general and may be reused by other applications with similar requirements; application specifications that adopt it as a base format should address the questions raised in the application design considerations.

The CPIM specification defines a number of operations to be supported and criteria to be satisfied for interworking between diverse instant messaging protocols. The intent is to allow a variety of different protocols to interwork through gateways to support cross-protocol messaging that meets the requirements of RFC 2779. To adequately meet those security requirements, a common message format is needed so that end-to-end signatures and encryption may be applied. The document describes a common canonical message format that must be used by any CPIM-compliant message transfer protocol, whereby signatures are calculated for end-to-end security.

The design is intended to enable security to be applied, while itself remaining agnostic about the specific security mechanisms that may be appropriate for a given application. For CPIM instant messaging and presence, specific security protocols are specified by the CPIM instant messaging and CPIM presence specifications. The message format described is not itself a MIME data format, although it may be contained within a MIME object and may contain MIME objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Several instant messaging protocols have to pass messages to each other through gateways. A message that has to be signed end to end cannot be rewritten along the way, so the protocols need one agreed format that survives the trip untouched.

sections.title: Why Not Plain Email Headers
sections.content:
RFC 2779 requires that an instant message can carry a MIME payload, so some level of support for MIME will be a common element of any CPIM compliant protocol. It therefore seems reasonable that a common message format should use an RFC 2822 and MIME-like syntax, as protocol implementations must already contain code to parse this. Unfortunately, using pure RFC 2822 and MIME can be problematic.

The lexical structure is irregular. RFC 2822 and MIME allow a number of optional encodings and multiple ways to encode a particular value; for example, comments may be encoded in multiple ways. For security purposes, a single encoding method must be defined as a basis for computing message digest values, and protocols that transmit data in a different format would otherwise lose information needed to verify a signature.

Internationalization is weak. RFC 2822 and MIME require header values to use 7-bit ASCII, which is problematic for encoding international character sets, and the mechanisms for language tagging in RFC 2822 and MIME headers are awkward to use and have limited applicability.

Messages are mutable. Because the addition, modification or removal of header information is not explicitly forbidden, many applications that process MIME content, such as MIME gateways, rebuild or restructure messages in transit. This obliterates most attempts at achieving security, such as signatures, leaving receiving applications unable to verify the data received.

There is no clear syntactic distinction between message metadata and message content. Extensibility is limited: X-headers are problematic because they may not be standardized, which leads to situations where a header starts out as experimental and then finds widespread application, resulting in a common usage that cannot be standardized. There is no support for structured information, only text string values. And some processors impose line length limitations.

The message format defined by the document overcomes some of these difficulties by having a simplified syntax that is generally compatible with the format accepted by RFC 2822 and MIME parsers, and by having a stricter syntax. It also defines mechanisms to support some desired features not covered by the RFC 2822 and MIME format specifications.

The goals are a securable end-to-end format for a message, that is, a canonical message format to serve as a basis for signature calculation rather than specified security mechanisms; independence of any specific application; the capability of conveying a range of different address types; the assumption of an 8-bit clean message-transfer protocol; evolvability, so that it is extensible by multiple parties; a clear separation of message metadata from message content; a simple, regular, easily parsed syntax; and a compact, low-overhead format for simple messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Email headers are too loose for this job. The same value can be written in several ways, which breaks the idea of a signature over the exact text, and gateways are allowed to tidy messages up as they pass them on, which breaks the signature entirely.

sections.title: The Overall Message Structure
sections.content:
The CPIM message format encapsulates arbitrary MIME message content together with message and content related metadata. This can optionally be signed or encrypted using MIME security multiparts in conjunction with an appropriate security scheme.

A Message/CPIM object is a two-part entity, where the first part contains the message metadata and the second part is the message content. The two parts are separated from the enclosing MIME header fields, and from each other, by blank lines. The message metadata header information obeys more stringent syntax rules than the MIME message content headers that may be carried within the message. The end of the message body is defined by the framing mechanism of the protocol used.

The message MIME headers identify the message as a CPIM-formatted message. The only required MIME header is Content-type: Message/CPIM; other MIME headers may be used as appropriate for the message transfer environment.

Message headers carry information relevant to the end-to-end transfer of the message from sender to receiver. They must not be modified, reformatted or reordered in transit, but in some circumstances they may be examined by a CPIM message transfer protocol. They serve a similar purpose to RFC 2822 message headers in email and have a similar but restricted allowable syntax. The basic syntax is Key: Value.

Several rules apply. The entire header must be contained on a single line, and the line terminator is not considered part of the header value. Only one header per line, and multiple headers must not be included on a single line. Processors should not impose any line-length limitations. There must not be any whitespace at the beginning or end of a line. UTF-8 character encoding must be used throughout, and the character sequence CR,LF (13,10) must be used to terminate each line. The header name contains only US-ASCII characters. The header must not contain any control characters (0-31); if a header value needs to represent control characters then the escape mechanism must be used. There must be a single space character following the header name and colon. Multiple headers using the same key are allowed, although specific header semantics may dictate only one occurrence of any particular header. Header names must match exactly, so From: and from: are different headers. If a header name is not recognized or not understood, the header should be ignored, subject to the Require header. Interpretation of header values is dependent on the particular header definition, and message processors must preserve all octets of all headers exactly and must not change the order of message headers.

The final section of a Message/CPIM is the MIME-encapsulated message content, which follows standard MIME formatting rules. The MIME content headers must include at least a Content-Type header, and the content may be any MIME type.
sections.plainLanguage: A CPIM message has two halves separated by a blank line. The first half is the metadata headers, the second is the content wrapped as a MIME object. Everything is in UTF-8, every header sits on one line, and nothing in the header half may be rewritten on the way.

sections.title: The Character Escape Mechanism
sections.content:
The escape mechanism must be used to code control characters in a header, those having Unicode code points in the range U+0000 to U+001f or U+007f. Rather than invent something completely new, the escape mechanism has been adopted from that used by the Java programming language. The escape mechanism is applied to a UCS-2 character, not to the octets of its UTF-8 coding, and mapping to and from UTF-8 coding is performed without regard for escape sequences or character coding. The header syntax is defined so that octets corresponding to control characters other than CR and LF do not appear in the output.

An arbitrary UCS-2 character is escaped using the form \uxxxx, where the backslash is U+005c, the u is the lower case letter U+0075, and xxxx is a sequence of exactly four hexadecimal digits. The hexadecimal number is the UCS code point value of the escaped character. Seven further special sequences are used: \ for the backslash, " for the double quote, \' for the single quote, \b for backspace, \t for tab, \n for linefeed and \r for carriage return.

When generating a message, the special sequences must be used to encode any occurrence of the backslash, backspace, tab, linefeed or carriage return that appears anywhere in a header. The sequence for the double quote must be used for any occurrence of a double quote within a string delimited by double quotes, and the sequence for the single quote for any occurrence of a single quote within a string delimited by single quotes. The single or double quote characters that delimit a string value must not be escaped. The general escape sequence must be used for any other control character in the ranges U+0000 to U+0007, U+000b to U+000c, U+000e to U+001f or U+007f that appears anywhere in a header. All other characters must not be represented using an escape sequence.

When processing a message, the escape sequence usage described must be recognized. Any other occurrence of an escape sequence described should be recognized and treated as an occurrence of the corresponding Unicode character. Any backslash character should be interpreted as introducing an escape sequence, any unrecognized escape sequence should be treated as an instance of the character following the backslash, and an isolated backslash that is the last character of a header should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Header values cannot contain raw control characters, because those would break the one-line rule and the signing. They are written with a backslash escape instead, in the same style Java uses, so that the sender and the receiver agree on exactly which bytes were meant.

sections.title: Namespaces and Required Features
sections.content:
The header extensibility framework is optional: if no header extensions are allowed by an application then these structures may never be used. An application that uses this message format is expected to define the set of headers that are required and allowed for that application. The framework is based on that provided for XML by XML namespaces. All headers are associated with a namespace, which is in turn associated with a globally unique URI.

Within a particular message instance, header names are associated with a particular namespace through the presence or absence of a namespace prefix, which is a leading part of the header name followed by a period. In the form prefix.header-name: header-value the prefix is the header name prefix and the header name is the name within the namespace associated with the prefix. In the form header-name: header-value the prefix is absent and the header name is associated with a default namespace. The Message/CPIM media type registration designates a default namespace for any headers that are not more explicitly associated with any namespace, and in most cases that default namespace is all that is needed.

A namespace is identified by a URI, used simply as a globally unique identifier with no requirement that it can be used for any other purpose. Any legal globally unique URI may be used, and it must be a full absolute URI; relative URIs and URI references containing fragment identifiers must not be used for this purpose.

Within a specific message, an NS header is used to declare a namespace prefix and associate it with a URI that identifies a namespace. Following that declaration, the combination of namespace prefix and header name indicates a globally unique identifier for the header, consisting of the namespace URI and the header name. A namespace prefix declaration must precede any use of that prefix. With the exception of any application-specific predefined namespace prefixes, a namespace prefix is strictly local to the message in which it occurs, and the actual prefix used has no global significance. An NS header without a header prefix name specifies a default namespace for subsequent headers.

The framework allows different implementers to create extension headers without the worry of header name duplication; each defines headers within their own namespace.

Sometimes it is necessary for the sender of a message to insist that some functionality is understood by the recipient. By using the mandatory-to-recognize indicator, a sender is notifying the recipient that it must understand the named header or feature in order to properly understand the message. A header or feature is indicated as being mandatory-to-recognize by a Require header. Multiple required header names may be listed in a single Require header, separated by commas. Indiscriminate use of Require headers could harm interoperability, and it is suggested that any implementer who defines required headers also publish the header specifications so other implementations can successfully interoperate. The Require header may also be used to indicate that some non-header semantics must be implemented by the recipient, even when it does not appear as a header.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mechanisms let the format grow. A namespace header ties a prefix to a URI, so two implementations can use different header names for the same idea without colliding. A Require header lets the sender insist that the recipient understands something before the message means anything.

sections.title: The Defined Headers
sections.content:
The specification defines a core set of headers that are available for use by applications; an application specification must indicate the headers that may be used, those that must be recognized, and those that must appear in any message. The header definitions fall into two categories: those that are part of the CPIM format extensibility framework, and those that have been based on similar headers in RFC 2822 and specified here with corresponding semantics. All headers defined here are associated with the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:cpim-headers:.

The From header indicates the sender or originator of a message. If present, the formal name identifies the person or real world name for the originator, and the URI indicates an address for the originator. The syntax is From: [ Formal-name ] "<" URI ">".

The To header indicates the recipient of a message, with the same formal name and URI structure, and multiple recipients may be indicated by including multiple To headers. The cc header indicates a courtesy copy recipient, again with multiple recipients allowed by multiple headers.

The DateTime header supplies the date and time at which the sender sent the message. One purpose is to provide protection against a replay attack, by allowing the recipient to know when the message was intended to be sent. The value is the sender's current time when the message was transmitted, using ISO 8601 date and time format as profiled in Date and Time on the Internet.

The Subject header supplies the sender's description of the topic or content of the message. The sending agent should specify the language parameter if it has any reasonable knowledge of the language used by the sender. A message header may indicate a language for its value by including ;lang=tag after the header name and colon. If the language parameter is not applied to a header, any human-readable text is assumed to use the language identified as i-default.

The NS header declares a namespace prefix that may be used in subsequent header names. The Require header indicates a header or feature that must be implemented or understood by the receiver for correct message processing. The required header or feature does not have to be used in the message, but for brevity it is recommended that an implementation does not issue the Require header for unused features.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven headers are defined: From, To, cc, DateTime, Subject, NS and Require. The first five carry the ordinary message metadata, and the last two handle extensions and insistences.

sections.title: Application Design Considerations
sections.content:
As defined, the Message/CPIM content type uses a default namespace URI and does not define any other implicit namespace prefixes. Applications that have different requirements should define and register a different MIME media type, specify the required default namespace URI, and define any implied namespace prefixes as part of the media type specification.

Applications using the specification must also specify all headers that must be recognized by implementations of the application, any headers that must be present in all messages created by the application, any headers that may appear more than once in a message and how they are to be interpreted, for example how to interpret multiple Subject headers with different language parameter values, and the security mechanisms and cryptography schemes to be used, including any mandatory-to-implement security provisions.

The goal of providing a definitive message format to which security mechanisms can be applied places some constraints on the design of applications that use it. Within a network of message transfer agents, an intermediate gateway must not change the Message/CPIM content in any way. This implies that headers cannot be changed or reordered, transfer encoding cannot be changed, and languages cannot be changed. Because Message/CPIM messages are immutable, any transfer agent that wants to modify the message should create a new Message/CPIM message with the modified header and with the original message as its content. The document compares this to real-world bill-of-lading handling, where each person in the chain attaches a new sheet to the message, so that anyone can validate the original message and see what has changed and who changed it by following the trail of amendments.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway must hand the message on untouched. If something in the chain needs to change the message, it makes a new message and puts the old one inside it, so the trail of changes stays visible.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Message/CPIM format is designed with security in mind. In particular it is designed to be used with MIME security multiparts for signatures and encryption. To this end, Message/CPIM messages must be considered immutable once created.

Because Message/CPIM messages are binary messages, due to UTF-8 encoding, if they are transmitted across non-8-bit-clean transports then the transfer agent must tunnel the entire message. Changing the message data encoding is not an option, which implies that the Message/CPIM must be encapsulated by the message transfer system and unencapsulated at the receiving end of the tunnel. The resulting message must not have data loss due to the encoding and unencoding of the message. For example, an application may choose to apply the MIME base64 content-transfer-encoding to the Message/CPIM object to meet this requirement.

The media type registration records that the content may contain signed data, so any transfer encoding must be exactly reversed before the content is processed, and that very strict adherence to the message format, including whitespace usage, may be needed to achieve interoperability between different instant messaging protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The format assumes it will be signed or encrypted, which means the bytes must survive the journey unchanged. Over an old transport that cannot carry 8-bit data, the whole message is tunneled rather than re-encoded.

viz.caption: What RFC 2822 and MIME could not offer

items.title: Irregular lexical structure
items.text: The same value can be written in several ways, so a digest computed over it may not match.

items.title: Weak internationalization
items.text: Header values must be 7-bit ASCII, and the language tagging mechanisms are awkward and of limited applicability.

items.title: Mutability
items.text: Gateways rebuild messages in transit, which destroys signatures and leaves receivers unable to verify what they got.

items.title: Message and payload separation
items.text: There is no clear syntactic distinction between message metadata and message content.

items.title: Limited extensibility
items.text: X-headers cannot be standardized, so a header can become widely used without ever getting a specification.

items.title: Text values only
items.text: There is no support for structured information.

items.title: Line length limits
items.text: Some processors impose line length limitations.

viz.caption: The escape sequences a CPIM header may use

data.title: Escape sequences
data.code:
Arbitrary character:  \uxxxx    four hexadecimal digits
Backslash:            \\
Double quote:         \"
Single quote:         \'
Backspace:            \b
Tab:                  \t
Linefeed:             \n
Carriage return:      \r

items.label: Sender
items.desc: Indicates the sender or originator of a message, as a formal name and a URI.

items.label: Recipient
items.desc: Indicates the recipient of a message. Multiple recipients need multiple To headers.

items.label: Courtesy copy
items.desc: Indicates a courtesy copy recipient of a message.

items.label: Time sent
items.desc: The date and time at which the sender sent the message, in ISO 8601 format. It helps protect against replay attacks.

items.label: Topic
items.desc: The sender's description of the topic or content of the message. It may carry a language parameter.

items.label: Namespace
items.desc: Declares a namespace prefix that may be used in subsequent header names.

items.label: Must understand
items.desc: Indicates a header or feature that must be implemented or understood by the receiver.

data.title: An example Message/CPIM message
data.code:
m: Content-type: Message/CPIM
s:
h: From: MR SANDERS <im:piglet@100akerwood.com>
h: To: Depressed Donkey <im:eeyore@100akerwood.com>
h: DateTime: 2000-12-13T13:40:00-08:00
h: Subject: the weather will be fine today
h: Subject:;lang=fr beau temps prevu pour aujourd'hui
h: NS: MyFeatures <mid:MessageFeatures@id.foo.com>
h: Require: MyFeatures.VitalMessageOption
h: MyFeatures.VitalMessageOption: Confirmation-requested
h: MyFeatures.WackyMessageOption: Use-silly-font
s:
e: Content-type: text/xml; charset=utf-8
e: Content-ID: <1234567890@foo.com>
e:
e: <body>
e: Here is the text of my message.
e: </body>
